newsitem.title: USA: Auto rebound bolsters industry in November.
newsitem.headline: Auto rebound bolsters industry in November.

text.p: Automakers resumed churning out new cars and trucks at a rapid pace in November, powering the nation's industrial output ahead at the fastest rate in nine months, the Federal Reserve said Monday.
Total output by the nation's factories, mines and utilities increased a sharper-than-expected 0.9 percent -- the largest monthly rise since a 1.3 percent gain in February.
Cold weather played a role, too, as gas and electric utilities boosted production strongly last month in response to strong consumer demand.
Industrial production fell a revised 0.2 percent in October instead of dropping 0.5 percent as first reported, the Fed said.

October industrial output was depressed because strikes in Canada against General Motors Corp. caused parts shortages that forced some U.S. auto plants to close briefly. The strike was settled and assembly lines were geared up last month.
"A rebound in the production of motor vehicles at strike-affected General Motors plants and in the production of related parts and materials accounted for about half of the gain," the Fed said.

Analysts said the concentration of the November rise in two industries -- auto and utilities -- made the monthly increase appear more dramatic than was warranted. It was seen as having little or no impact on Fed policy-makers, who meet Tuesday to consider interest-rate strategy.
The Federal Open Market Committee is widely expected to once again leave interest rates unchanged in the absence of clear signs of inflation pressures.

"It's consistent with a moderate pace of economic growth," said economist Cynthia Latta of DRI/McGraw Hill Inc. in Lexington, Mass., "But there's no sign that we're pushing hard against the limits of capacity."
During November, U.S. industry ran at 83.3 percent of maximum capacity, up from 82.9 percent in September but still under the year's peak of 83.7 percent reached in June.
"I don't think that will affect (Federal Reserve policy-makers') considerations at all," Latta said. "There's still no sign of inflation because there just isn't much pricing power right now."
Production by utilities companies increased 2.5 percent last month after a slim 0.3 percent rise in October. Mining output was up 0.1 percent in November following a 0.6 percent drop in October.
The pickup in vehicle assembly rates was striking after a relatively slack October.

New cars were churned out at a rate of 6.3 million a year in November, compared with 5.5 million in October, while production of light trucks increased to 5.6 million a year from 5.4 million in October.
Largely as a result of the auto industry rebound, manufacturing output grew 0.8 percent in November after contracting 0.2 percent in October.
The Fed said that, excluding motor vehicles and parts, November industrial output was up 0.6 percent following a 0.3 percent October increase.
There was a substantial increase in production of commercial aircraft during November and a moderate rise in output of computers and other information processing equipment, the Fed said.
Economist David Orr of First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C., noted there were also increases in production of goods ranging from lumber, furniture and fabricated metals to tobacco and food products.

"Businesses must be relatively comfortable with their inventory levels," Orr said. But he added that if sales slow as expected after Christmas, then stocks of unsold goods could become a problem by spring that would put a drag on production next year.
